data.text:
THE CPP-NPA-NDF CONTRADICTION: ANTI-IMPERIALIST RHETORIC, NEOLIBERAL ALIGNMENT

At the Munich Security Conference, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a speech that dispensed with diplomatic subtlety and revived the language of civilizational supremacy.

Socialism was framed as a primary adversary, and the narrative revolved around restoring Western dominance, cultural cohesion, and geopolitical primacy.

Beneath the rhetoric of alliance and shared heritage was a clear strategic proposition. Europe must consolidate behind Washington to preserve what he described as the West’s historic leadership. Stripped of ornamentation, the address read as an appeal to reinvigorate Western hegemony over the Global South. An updated imperial posture presented as “strategic cooperation.”

The historical irony is difficult to ignore. For centuries, Western expansion was justified in the language of civilization, order, and destiny. Today, similar themes reappear under the banner of security and renewal. What is being defended is not merely culture or stability, but a hierarchy of power that has long structured global economic and political relations.

In this context, the theater of certain self-proclaimed revolutionary movements in the Philippines, such as the CPP-NPA-NDF, becomes increasingly untenable. Groups that once claimed to wage anti-imperialist struggle have, in practice, operated within a framework shaped by Western liberal institutions, funding streams, and discursive paradigms.

These are the same groups that publicly endorsed the transfer of a fellow Filipino to a foreign tribunal, cheering as external institutions asserted jurisdiction over our domestic affairs. 

Their agitation often mirrors the ideological priorities of the very Western centers they rhetorically oppose.

If Washington openly defines socialism as an enemy while simultaneously weaponizing liberal norms to maintain influence abroad, then movements that reduce politics to performative protest reveal their contradictions.

Anti-imperialism cannot survive as branding.

It requires a coherent economic program, an independent foreign policy, and strategic alignment that advances national development rather than reproducing dependency.

The global order is shifting toward multipolarity. Attempts to resurrect a unipolar Western century will encounter resistance not because of ideology alone, but because the material center of gravity has already begun to move.

Any serious political movement must reckon with that reality instead of reenacting scripts that history has already outgrown.
